title: Psalm 105: He Remembers His Covenant Forever
summary: A call to give thanks and make God's deeds known leads into a retelling of Israel's early history as the story of God keeping his promise to Abraham. God protected the wandering patriarchs, sent Joseph ahead into Egypt, multiplied Israel there, sent Moses and Aaron with plagues, brought the people out with silver and gold, guided and fed them in the wilderness, and gave them the land, so that they might keep his statutes and obey his laws.
story: Psalms 105 and 106 close Book IV of the Psalter as a pair, two retellings of the same history from opposite sides. Psalm 105 tells it as the story of God's faithfulness; Psalm 106 will tell it as the story of Israel's unfaithfulness. Coming after the creation hymn of Psalm 104, Psalm 105 moves from God's care for every creature to his particular promise to one family. Book IV has been answering the collapse of David's kingdom and the exile by looking back to Moses and the older covenant. This psalm reaches even further, to Abraham, and insists that the promise of the land is an everlasting covenant that God remembers.
historical:
The psalm has no heading. Its first fifteen verses appear, with small differences, in 1 Chronicles 16:8-22, as part of the song sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem; the rest of that song draws on Psalms 96 and 106. Scholars debate whether the Chronicler, writing after the exile, assembled existing psalms for the scene or drew on a tradition that the song went back to David's time. Many date Psalm 105 itself to the period after the exile, when a people who had lost the land needed to hear that God's promise of it was everlasting; others place it earlier in temple worship. It names no event of its own time.

The psalm's history follows Genesis and Exodus closely, with its own emphases. It covers the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), the famine and Joseph's slavery and rise (Genesis 37 to 47), Israel's growth and oppression in Egypt, and the plagues, exodus, and wilderness provision (Exodus 7 to 17). It lists eight plagues rather than ten, starting with darkness (the ninth in Exodus) and omitting the death of livestock and the boils, and it says nothing of Sinai or of Israel's rebellions. The selection serves its purpose: God's word always came true.
cultural:
The psalm assumes the social world of Genesis. The patriarchs were “strangers in the land” (verse 12), resident outsiders without property rights, moving with their flocks among the settled kingdoms of Canaan and Egypt. Such people were vulnerable, which is why the psalm stresses that God rebuked kings on their behalf, recalling the stories of Pharaoh and Abimelech and the patriarchs' wives (Genesis 12 and 20). Calling the patriarchs “My anointed ones” and “My prophets” (verse 15) applies to them titles normally used for kings and prophets: they were set apart and under God's protection.

Egypt is called “the land of Ham” (verses 23 and 27), following the table of nations in Genesis 10:6, where Mizraim (Egypt) is a son of Ham. Joseph's rise from prisoner to steward of Pharaoh's household fits the Egyptian practice of appointing high officials over the royal estate, though no Egyptian record names him. The final verse gives the purpose of the whole history: the land was given so that Israel would keep God's statutes and laws, the plural of torah, instruction.
literary: The psalm opens with a burst of commands in verses 1 to 6 (give thanks, call, make known, sing, tell, glory, seek, remember), addressed to the offspring of Abraham. Verses 7 to 11 state the theme: God remembers his covenant. The rest retells history in episodes: the patriarchs (verses 12 to 15), Joseph (verses 16 to 22), Israel in Egypt (verses 23 to 25), Moses and the plagues (verses 26 to 36), and the exodus and wilderness (verses 37 to 41). Verse 42 closes the frame by repeating the theme, “For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant”. Remembering is the key: Israel is told to remember in verse 5, and God is said to remember in verses 8 and 42. God is the subject of almost every verb in the history; human beings barely act.

outline.t: Give thanks, seek him, and remember his wonders
The everlasting covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
The patriarchs protected among the nations
Joseph sent ahead, tested, and raised up
Israel in Egypt, Moses and Aaron, and the plagues
Brought out with joy, fed, and given the land

doctrines.note: The psalm's spine is God's covenant with Abraham, confirmed to Isaac and Jacob and remembered “forever”. History unfolds as God keeping his word, even through famine, slavery, and oppression.
God “called down famine” and “sent a man before them”, Joseph, sold as a slave. The psalm reads even disaster and injustice as within God's purposes, echoing Joseph's own words in Genesis 50:20.
The last verse says why the land was given: “that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws”. Grace comes first, and obedience is the response it makes possible, not the price of it.

words.note: Zakar, to remember. In Hebrew, remembering is not merely recalling a fact but acting on it. When God remembers his covenant, he moves to fulfill it; when Israel remembers his wonders, it responds in worship and trust.

Mashiach, anointed one, the word from which Messiah comes. Usually used of kings and priests, it is applied in verse 15 to the patriarchs as people God had set apart and protected. It shows the word's range before it became a title for the coming king.

Tsaraph, to refine or test, used of smelting metal. Verse 19 says the word of the LORD tested Joseph (the BSB renders it as proving him right). Joseph's years in chains are pictured as a refining process.
Berit, covenant, a binding commitment between parties, often sealed by an oath. The psalm calls God's covenant with the patriarchs everlasting and links it to the gift of the land of Canaan.

christ: When Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, praised God at the birth of his son, he said that God had remembered his holy covenant, the oath he swore to our father Abraham (Luke 1:72-73), language very close to verses 8, 9, and 42 of this psalm. The New Testament sees God's promise to Abraham reaching its fulfillment in Christ, the offspring through whom the blessing of Abraham comes to the nations (Galatians 3:8, 14, 16). The psalm's picture of Joseph, sold by his brothers, suffering unjustly, and then raised to rule and save many, has also long been read as a pattern that anticipates Christ, though the New Testament does not draw that parallel explicitly. Here the link is typological, a shape in the story rather than a stated prediction.

hard.q: Verse 25 says God turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate his people. Does God cause people to do evil?
hard.a: The line is jarring, and it belongs to a wider biblical pattern, including the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in Exodus. The psalm's point is that even Egypt's hostility did not fall outside God's rule; Israel's oppression, like Joseph's slavery, was taken up into his purpose. Interpreters differ on how to hold this together with human responsibility. Some emphasize that God works through people's existing choices, giving them over to what they already want (Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that God hardened it). Others stress God's sovereignty more strongly and see it as a mystery beyond full explanation. Scripture holds both that God is sovereign and that people are accountable for the evil they do, without resolving every question about how.

questions: The psalm tells Israel's story with God as the main actor and barely mentions human failures. What would change if you told your own life story that way?
Joseph waited in chains until God's word came true. How do you think about waiting when God's promises seem slow?
The last verse says the land was given so that Israel would keep God's laws. How does receiving grace shape the way you obey?
